title: Susceptibility-kinetic uncertainty relations for quantum systems
authors: Didrik Palmqvist, Ludovico Tesser, Janine Splettstoesser
abstract: Kinetic uncertainty relations bound current precision of stochastic processes by dynamical activity. The extension of these bounds to quantum systems has been impeded by coherence, strong system-reservoir coupling, and the subtlety of defining dynamical activity in the quantum regime. Here, we introduce a partial dynamical activity through the quantum Fisher information associated with the rescaling of the system-reservoir coupling and show that it bounds current precision via a universal susceptibility-kinetic uncertainty relation. The general validity of this relation for any open quantum system is guaranteed by the natural contribution of a susceptibility term, which is experimentally accessible by tuning the system-reservoir coupling strength. We show how the partial dynamical activity encompasses previous definitions of activity in the weak-coupling Markovian limit and that it provides an information-geometric interpretation of correlator-based activities. We illustrate the tight constraint on precision that our bound provides with the example of steady-state transport through a double quantum dot, where quantum effects invalidate previously developed kinetic uncertainty relations. We expect our bound to provide a powerful tool for optimizing precision in arbitrary quantum systems.
summary: The paper introduces the Susceptibility-Kinetic Uncertainty Relation (S-KUR) as a universal bound governing current precision in open quantum systems. By defining Partial Dynamical Activity using quantum Fisher information, it overcomes limitations of previous bounds that failed under strong coupling or coherence. This tool is demonstrated to be robustly applicable to complex transport phenomena like those in double quantum dots.
main_problem: The central problem is establishing universal uncertainty relations that constrain current precision for open quantum systems operating out of equilibrium.
main_result: The authors derive the Susceptibility-Kinetic Uncertainty Relation (S-KUR), a general bound on current precision derived from partial dynamical activity, which remains valid even when standard kinetic uncertainty relations fail due to quantum coherence or strong coupling.
method: The relation is derived using the Quantum Cramér-Rao Bound applied to the response of an observable to changes in system-reservoir coupling strength ($	heta$), leading to the definition of Partial Dynamical Activity (PDA).
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on open quantum systems coupled to reservoirs, exemplified by transport through a Double Quantum Dot (DQD) structure. The dynamics are governed by time-dependent Hamiltonians and analyzed in the steady-state limit.
key_observables: Current ($\hat{J}(\hat{X})$), Susceptibility term ($\dot{M}(\hat{X})$), Zero-frequency noise ($S(\hat{X})$), Partial Dynamical Activity ($A_V(t)$).
important_parameters: Coupling strength ($	heta$), Bias voltage ($\Delta\mu$), Temperature ($T$), and the time evolution parameter $t$.
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on defining PDA via quantum Fisher information related to coupling rescaling, and in some analyses, approximations like the secular approximation or Markovian limits are used.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the failure of classical local KURs compared to the saturation of the S-KUR for particle current in a DQD across varying bias; another figure shows the disappearance of classical bound violations upon increasing temperature.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the problem using the QCRB, introducing PDA via quantum Fisher information, deriving the universal S-KUR, and then validating this relation by applying it to complex physical examples like steady-state transport in a DQD under various bias and temperature conditions.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, general theoretical tool for quantifying fundamental limits on measurement precision in non-equilibrium quantum transport, which is highly relevant to mesoscopic physics and quantum thermodynamics.
